ideas.title: What good looks like today: lessons from the organisations ahead of the game
ideas.standfirst: Airline crews, medical simulation centres, the US Army, Harvard Business School, Duolingo, Khan Academy and Outward Bound are often held up as the best in the world at helping people learn. Put them side by side and the same few habits keep appearing. This is what they share, what the evidence says about each, and what is worth borrowing.

short.heading: The short version
items: **They rehearse the hard part, not the whole job.** Aviation and medicine put people through the rare, costly moments in a simulator, again and again, before those moments happen for real.
**They talk about it straight afterwards.** The after-action review, the flight debrief and the case discussion all make people say what happened and why before anyone gives a verdict.
**They bring it back.** Recurrent training, spaced recall and mastery checks all assume that one exposure is not enough.
**Their reputations run ahead of their evidence.** Most have good evidence for the method they use and much weaker evidence for their own results. Borrow the method, not the brand.

sections.h: Habit one: rehearse the moments that matter
p: **Airline crews practise emergencies as a whole crew.** Under US rules, line-oriented flight training uses a complete crew in a full flight simulator, includes abnormal and emergency procedures, and is briefed before and after. Medical simulation centres do the same for clinical skills. A pooling of 14 studies found simulation with deliberate practice beat traditional clinical education.

**The lesson is to find the hard part and give it most of the time.** Neither aviation nor medicine spends its simulator hours on the routine. They pick the moments where a mistake is rare, expensive and hard to practise at work. Most workplace training does the opposite and covers everything once. There is more on [rehearsing what could go wrong](t:4.13) and on [building practice at the edge of ability](t:1.6).

sections.h: Habit two: debrief before you judge
p: **The US Army's after-action review asks the group what happened and why before anyone gives a view.** A pooling of 46 samples found debriefs of this kind improved later performance by about a fifth to a quarter, and facilitated debriefs did better. Harvard Business School's case method works on a related idea: people must commit to a decision before the discussion, which makes the discussion matter to them.

**What these share is that the learner does the thinking first.** The facilitator's job is to make it safe to say what really happened and to keep the talk on what to do next time. There is more on [debriefing an activity](t:4.28) and on [using problems and cases when judgement is the goal](t:2.15).

sections.h: Habit three: one go is never enough
p: **Every one of these organisations assumes people forget.** Aviation writes refreshers into the rules, with some drills repeated at fixed intervals. Duolingo's model estimates when each learner is about to forget a word and brings it back. Khan Academy asks learners to show they can do a skill before moving on. Outward Bound's strongest results came from courses of 20 days or more, not from a single day.

**This is the habit most workplace training lacks.** A one-off event with nothing after it is still the norm. The organisations held up as models plan the second, third and tenth exposure before the first one ends. There is more on [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4) and on [planning refreshers before skills fade](t:5.19).

sections.h: Habit four: stretch people together, away from routine
p: **Outward Bound takes groups away and sets them a goal that feels too hard.** A 1997 pooling of 96 studies found gains in outcomes such as self-concept and leadership that grew slightly at follow-up, which is unusual. The gains were in confidence and personal skills, not job skills, and results varied widely between programmes.

**This is the closest of the seven to a training retreat, and the most cautious result.** It supports taking people away to stretch them together. It does not support promising that a short retreat will change how they work. There is more in [Why take people away?](insight:why-take-people-away)

sections.h: What the evidence does not show
p: **The strong evidence is for the methods, not the organisations.** Debriefs, simulation with deliberate practice, spaced recall and mastery learning all have good research behind them, much of it from outside the organisations that made them famous. We found no independent study of results at Harvard Business School itself. Duolingo's best-known efficacy study was paid for by Duolingo, and the one independent study was tiny. Khan Academy's usage studies are correlations. Aviation's crew training changes attitudes and behaviour more clearly than it changes accident rates.

**That is a reason to borrow with confidence, not a reason to dismiss them.** The habits are sound. The halo is not evidence. When a client says they want to train like an airline, the useful reply is to ask which habit they mean and whether they will pay for the repetition that makes it work.

mind.heading: What to borrow for your own work
items: **Pick the hard moment and give it the time.** Ask the client which situation goes wrong most expensively, and build the practice around that.
**Debrief every exercise, and ask before you tell.** Protect the debrief time in the timetable. It is the part that always wants to be cut.
**Plan the second exposure before the first.** Put the follow-up, the recall questions and the refresher in the calendar while people are still in the room.
**Check that people can do it, not that they were there.** A short observed task beats an attendance list.
**Quote the method, not the brand.** "Debriefs improved later performance by about a fifth" is a claim you can defend. "We train like the Army" is not.

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **A retreat is good at three of the four habits.** It gives time to rehearse the hard part, time to debrief properly, and a group that will hold each other to a standard. It is weak at the fourth, bringing it back, because it is one block. Selling the follow-up as part of the retreat, rather than an optional extra, is what turns a good event into something that looks like the organisations people admire.

ideas.title: The offsite and retreat market: who is buying, and what they want now
ideas.standfirst: Companies are spending on getting people together again, but they want the time to count. This piece gathers what the industry surveys and one large employer's own data say about demand for offsites and retreats, and what that means for someone setting up to run them.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Confidence in business events is the highest in five years.** In Amex GBT's survey of 601 meeting professionals, 85% were optimistic about 2026, up from 74% a year earlier. Costs are rising too.

**Buyers want experiences that people remember and that change something.** Creating engaging experiences was the planners' top priority, and the same report asks whether events should be judged on return on experience as well as return on investment.

**Distributed companies are paying to bring teams together on purpose.** Atlassian's data on its own staff found intentional gatherings lifted team connection by 27%, and the lift lasted four to five months.

**Wellness is growing, but not as a workplace perk.** Wellness tourism is forecast to grow about 9% a year. Spending on workplace wellness programmes was the only part of the wellness economy that shrank.

sections.h: Demand for getting together is back
p: **Planners are more optimistic than at any point in five years.** American Express Global Business Travel's 2026 forecast is based on a YouGov survey of 601 meeting professionals in eight countries, carried out in July 2025. 85% said they were optimistic or very optimistic about the year ahead, against 74% the year before. The same report lists rising costs as a concern and says AI is becoming part of every stage of planning.

**The priority has moved from logistics to experience.** The report names creating engaging experiences as the top priority, and asks whether events should be judged on return on experience as well as return on investment. That is a planners' survey, not a buyers' survey, so it tells you what the industry thinks clients want. It fits what L&D buyers say: they want time together that does something the office and a video call cannot.

sections.h: Why distributed companies are buying gatherings
p: **Atlassian measured what its own gatherings did.** Since 2020 its staff have chosen where they work, and the company now brings whole teams together in person three or four times a year, each gathering with a clear purpose. Across more than 1,600 gatherings with an average of 16 people, team connection rose by 27% afterwards and stayed higher for four to five months. New hires and graduates gained most, and their sense of connection also faded fastest.

**It is one company's data on its own staff, so treat it as a strong example rather than a law.** It is also the clearest published evidence that a planned gathering does more for connection than people drifting into an office. For a retreat business, two details matter: the effect fades within a season, which is an argument for a programme of gatherings rather than a one-off, and newcomers benefit most, which is an argument for onboarding cohorts. There is more on [designing a course so people leave connected](t:5.10).
**The wellness economy keeps growing.** The Global Wellness Institute put it at $6.8 trillion in 2024, up 7.9% in a year, and forecast wellness tourism to grow about 9% a year to 2029.

**Workplace wellness was the one sector that shrank,** with global spending down 1.5% from 2023 to 2024. One reading is that employers are cooling on standalone wellness perks while individuals spend more on their own wellbeing. A retreat sold as a wellness benefit is selling into the weak part of that market. A retreat sold as development, with good food, sleep, movement and time outdoors as part of how it works, sits closer to what is growing. There is more on [describing the retreat honestly](t:9.7).
**Purpose before venue.** Atlassian's rule is that every gathering has a clear purpose, group and structure. Buyers increasingly ask what the time is for before they ask where it is.

**Evidence of something changing.** The pressure on L&D to show results has not gone away, and the Amex report's talk of return on experience shows planners feel it too. A retreat that can show what people did differently afterwards will win against one that can only show a satisfaction score. There is more in [What the best learning teams measure](insight:what-the-best-learning-teams-measure).
**Less drinking, more choice.** Fewer young adults drink, and alcohol-free options are now expected. There is more in [Drinking less](insight:drinking-less-and-the-work-event).

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **Industry optimism is not your pipeline.** These surveys describe the sector. Your first clients will come from people who already trust you.
**Sell a programme, not a trip.** The Atlassian effect faded within a season. Two or three gatherings a year, with work in between, is the stronger offer.
**Costs are rising for everyone.** Venues, food and travel are going up. Price with a margin that survives a bad quarter. There is more on [pricing a retreat](t:9.12).
**Do not sell wellness to the wellness budget.** That budget is the one shrinking. Sell development that happens to be good for people.

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **The opening is real, and it is specific.** Distributed and hybrid companies need their teams together a few times a year and want those days to count. New managers, new hires and teams after a reorganisation gain most. A small business that designs the purpose, runs the time well and follows up afterwards is offering exactly what large event agencies are least set up to do.

ideas.title: AI and learning: what the 2025–26 evidence shows
ideas.standfirst: The first good experiments on AI and learning are in, and they point two ways. AI built to tutor can help people learn faster. AI used to get the answer can raise performance today and lower it tomorrow. This piece gathers the studies that matter and what they mean for training design.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Doing better with AI is not the same as learning.** In a field experiment with about 1,000 Turkish secondary pupils, ChatGPT access raised practice scores by 48%, and pupils who had used it then scored 17% worse on an exam without it.
**Design changes the result.** The same study's tutor version, which gave hints rather than answers, raised practice scores by 127% and largely avoided the harm.

**A tutor built on good teaching can beat a good class.** At Harvard, students learned more than twice as much in less time from a purpose-built AI tutor as from an active-learning class on the same topic.
**Trust in the tool lowers the thinking.** Knowledge workers who trusted AI more reported less critical thinking. Those confident in their own skill reported more.

p: **The clearest experiment so far comes from secondary schools in Turkey.** Bastani and colleagues gave about 1,000 pupils either a standard ChatGPT interface, a version set up as a tutor, or nothing, during maths practice. With standard ChatGPT, practice scores rose by 48%. When the AI was taken away for the exam, those pupils scored 17% worse than pupils who had never had it. The tutor version, which was prompted to give hints rather than answers, raised practice scores by 127% and largely removed the harm on the exam.

**The OECD has made this its headline.** Its Digital Education Outlook 2026 concludes that general-purpose AI tools can improve performance on tasks without leading to learning, and that learning gains appear when AI is used with a clear teaching purpose. For training, the lesson is direct: if people use AI to do the exercise, the exercise stops teaching. There is more on [guarding against over-reliance](t:7.12).

sections.h: When AI is built to teach
p: **A Harvard physics experiment found a purpose-built tutor beat a strong class.** Kestin and colleagues ran a crossover trial with 194 students in an introductory physics course. Each student learned one topic in an active-learning class and another at home with an AI tutor built on the same teaching principles. Students learned more than twice as much in less time with the tutor, and reported feeling more engaged.

**The comparison was with a good class, which is what makes it striking.** It was also one course, at one university, with well-prepared students and a tutor written by the course team. The authors say it should not be read as AI beating teachers in general. What it shows is that the design principles that work in a room, such as working through problems, getting feedback and not being handed the answer, also work when an AI delivers them. There is more on [using AI as a practice partner](t:7.10) and on [expecting moderate gains from adaptive tools](t:7.2).

sections.h: What it does to thinking at work
p: **Confidence in the tool goes with less checking.** A Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon survey of 319 knowledge workers, covering 936 real examples of AI use, found that higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking, and higher confidence in one's own ability went with more. People described their effort moving from producing work to checking and combining what the AI produced.

**It is a self-report survey, not an experiment.** It shows a pattern in how people describe their work, not proof that AI weakens thinking. It does suggest who needs training most: people new to a task, who are least able to judge the AI's answer and most likely to accept it. There is more on [training people to check the AI's work](t:7.4).

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **Decide what the learner must be able to do without AI.** Then design the practice so the AI cannot do that part for them.
**Set AI up as a tutor, not an answer machine.** Prompts that give hints, ask questions and hold back the answer are the difference the Turkish study measured.
**Test without the tool.** If the job will be done with AI, assess with it too. If the skill must stand alone, assess without it.
**Most of this evidence is from schools and universities.** Workplace trials are still scarce. Expect the direction to hold and the sizes to differ.

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **A retreat is one of the few places where people practise without the tool in their hand.** That is worth saying plainly to buyers. Live practice, debate and feedback build the judgement people need to check AI's work. AI can still play a part, as a practice partner between sessions or a tutor in the follow-up, set up to coach rather than to answer. There is more on [setting a rule for AI in the room](t:7.9).

ideas.title: Drinking less: what the change in drinking means for work events and retreats
ideas.standfirst: A quarter of adults in England now do not drink, and young adults are leading the change. The bar tab used to be the centre of the work social. This piece sets out what has changed, what employers are responsible for, and how to run evenings that work for everyone.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Not drinking is now common.** In the Health Survey for England 2024, 24% of adults said they had not drunk alcohol in the past year, up from about 19% through 2011 to 2022. Among 16 to 24-year-olds it was about a third.
**Alcohol-free drinks are a growing market, not a novelty.** Alcohol-free volumes are forecast to grow by more than a third to 2029 across the leading markets.
**A work event is still work.** Employers keep a duty of care at work socials, and can be held responsible for what happens there.
**Design the evening around something other than the bar.** Food, a fire, a walk, a game or a conversation give everyone a reason to stay.

p: **Fewer people drink at all.** The Health Survey for England 2024 asked thousands of adults about their drinking. 24% said they had not drunk alcohol in the past year, against a long-standing level of about 19%. The change is driven by younger people, and by young men in particular, with about a third of 16 to 24-year-olds not drinking.

**Those who drink, drink differently.** Drinkaware's survey of 18 to 24-year-olds found the share not drinking rose from 14% in 2017 to 21% in 2023, and those who do drink do so less often. It also found the young adults who drink are more likely than other ages to drink at high-risk levels. Both groups will be at your event.

**The drinks have caught up.** IWSR expected alcohol-free beer, wine and spirits to grow 9% in volume in 2025 across the leading markets, and by 36% to 2029. The British Beer and Pub Association called 2025 a record year for low and no-alcohol beer in the UK. A good alcohol-free option is now expected, not a favour.

**A work social is treated as part of work.** Employment lawyers and Acas guidance agree that an employer keeps a duty of care at events it organises, including evenings and parties. Employers have been held responsible for harassment and other conduct at work socials. Acas suggests plenty of food and non-alcoholic drinks, thinking about how people get home, and making clear that normal standards of behaviour apply. This is not legal advice. Check the current guidance or take advice for your situation.

**On a residential, the evening is part of the programme.** If people are expected to stay, the employer and the organiser share the responsibility for what the programme asks of them. There is more on [setting the rules for evenings, alcohol and free time](t:8.14) and on [writing the duty-of-care plan first](t:8.5).

**Put something other than the bar at the centre.** A long meal, a fire, a walk at dusk, a quiz or a guest's story all give people a reason to stay that has nothing to do with drinking. There is more on [running evenings and fireside conversations](t:8.30).

**Make not drinking invisible.** Good alcohol-free drinks served the same way as the rest, with nobody asking why. People do not drink for many reasons, including health, faith, pregnancy, recovery, medication and preference, and none of them is the group's business.
**Protect the morning.** The programme should never depend on a late night. Sleep matters for what people learned the day before. There is more on [protecting sleep on multi-day programmes](t:1.12).

items: **Do not make the evening alcohol-free by decree unless the client wants it.** Many people enjoy a drink. The aim is an evening that does not depend on it.
**Brief the venue.** Ask for the alcohol-free list in advance and check it is more than soft drinks.

**Put the bar in the risk assessment.** Late bars, fires and water do not mix. There is more on [planning for incidents](t:8.15).

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **This trend suits a retreat in nature.** Evenings built around food, fire, walks and conversation are what a rural retreat does well, and they appeal to the people who no longer want a work night out in a bar. Say so in how you describe the retreat: a programme where the evenings are part of the experience and nobody has to drink to belong.

ideas.title: Neuroinclusion: designing training for different minds
ideas.standfirst: About one in seven people in the UK are thought to be neurodivergent, and many never tell their employer. In any group you train, some people process information, attention, noise and social demands differently. This piece gathers the UK research, the legal basics and the design choices that help.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Assume neurodivergent people are in every room.** Acas puts the estimate at about one in seven, and many are undiagnosed or have not disclosed.
**Many do not feel supported at work.** In a CIPD survey, only 37% of neurodivergent employees said their organisation gave meaningful support, and 31% had not told their manager or HR.
**Design for the range first, adjust for individuals second.** Flexible design helps everyone and avoids making people ask. The research on it is promising but limited.
**The law asks for reasonable adjustments.** Where a condition meets the Equality Act's definition of disability, employers must make reasonable adjustments. This is not legal advice.

p: **Neurodivergence is common.** Acas says about one in seven people in the UK are neurodivergent, a term that covers conditions such as ADHD, autism, dyslexia and dyspraxia. It is an estimate, and it includes many people without a diagnosis.

**Many people keep it to themselves.** The CIPD and Uptimize surveyed 1,047 employees in 2023, 790 of whom identified as neurodivergent. 31% of neurodivergent respondents had not told their manager or HR, and among the reasons was worry that people would make assumptions based on stereotypes. Neurodivergent respondents were more likely to say they often felt exhausted at work (45% against 30%) and lonely (23% against 17%). One in five said they had experienced harassment or discrimination because of their neurodivergence. The sample was not weighted and is not representative of all employees, so read the figures as signals, not national rates.

**Managers often do not know what to do.** Acas research found 59% of line managers did not know how to make a reasonable adjustment for a neurodivergent employee. Trainers are often in the same position. There is more on [finding out who is in the room before you design](t:1.29).

**Universal Design for Learning plans for different needs from the start.** It offers more than one way to take in information, more than one way to take part and more than one way to show what you have learned. A 2023 meta-analysis of 20 studies found a moderate positive effect on achievement, about 0.43 of a standard deviation, across learners from pre-school to adults. An earlier review found UDL improved the learning process but had not shown an effect on outcomes, and critics point out how few rigorous studies there are. Treat it as a sound way to plan, with promising evidence, rather than a proven method. There is more on [designing for different minds from the start](t:2.23) and on [designing for the range of people, not the average](t:2.16).

**Small choices remove most of the friction.** Send the agenda and materials in advance. Say what each session will ask people to do. Give instructions in writing as well as aloud. Offer a choice of ways to take part, such as writing instead of speaking, or observing a role-play before joining one. Keep a quiet space. Avoid surprises, such as cold-calling or unannounced performance. None of this needs anyone to disclose anything. There is more on [telling learners what to expect](t:2.21) and on [running a role-play people do not dread](t:4.29).

**Reasonable adjustments are a duty, not a favour.** Under the Equality Act 2010, where a condition meets the definition of disability and a person is put at a substantial disadvantage, employers must make reasonable adjustments. What counts as reasonable depends on the situation. Acas guidance gives examples such as flexible hours, quiet spaces, noise-cancelling headphones and written instructions, many of them free or cheap. Training and assessment are covered. This is not legal advice. Check the current Acas guidance or take advice for a specific case.

**Ask everyone, not only those who disclose.** A joining question such as "Is there anything that would help you take part fully?" sent to every participant collects what you need without singling anyone out. There is more on [collecting only the learner data you need](t:9.16).

**Inclusion helps everyone.** Clear instructions, a quiet space and no surprises make training better for the whole group.

p: **A retreat asks more of people than a training day.** Shared rooms, long days, group meals, noise and a full social calendar can be hard for some neurodivergent people, and they may not say so. ideas.title: Does coaching work? What the trials say
ideas.standfirst: Coaching is now a five-billion-dollar profession, and much of it is paid for by employers. The research has caught up a little: there are now enough randomised trials to pool. This piece sets out what they show, where they are weak, and how coaching fits around training.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Workplace coaching has a moderate effect in randomised trials.** A 2023 pooling of 37 trials found an average effect of about 0.6 of a standard deviation.
**The effect is real but probably smaller than it looks.** The same analysis found signs that positive studies are more likely to be published, and many outcomes are self-reported.
**It helps most with goals and self-management.** An earlier pooling found the largest effects on goal-directed self-regulation and the smallest on coping.
**Coaching is the strongest follow-up to training.** It works on the problem training is weakest at: using the skill back at work.

p: **The best evidence comes from randomised trials alone.** De Haan and Nilsson pooled 37 randomised controlled trials of workplace and executive coaching published between 1994 and 2021, with 2,528 participants in total. Coaching had a significant effect across leadership and personal outcomes, with a best estimate of about 0.59 of a standard deviation, which is moderate. They also found signs of publication bias, which usually means the true effect is somewhat smaller.

**Earlier work found the same direction.** Theeboom, Beersma and van Vianen's 2014 meta-analysis looked at five kinds of outcome. Coaching had positive effects on all of them, from 0.43 for coping to 0.74 for goal-directed self-regulation, which covers setting goals and working towards them. Performance and skills, wellbeing and attitudes to work sat in between.
**Many outcomes are what coachees say about themselves.** Ratings by managers or business results are rarer, and smaller. A trial with outside ratings is worth more than several without.

**Coaching is not one thing.** The trials cover different coaches, methods, numbers of sessions and people. A pooled average tells you coaching can work. It does not tell you a particular coach or programme will. The relationship between coach and coachee keeps coming up as important, though which ingredients matter most is still argued over.

**The profession is growing faster than the evidence.** The International Coaching Federation's 2025 study estimated 122,974 coach practitioners worldwide and $5.34 billion in annual revenue, up 17% since 2023. Many coaches also train and facilitate. Growth says coaching is in demand. It says nothing about any one coach's results.

**Coaching works on transfer, which is training's weak point.** Training teaches the skill in a room. Coaching helps a person use it in their own job, with their own obstacles, over weeks. That makes a few coaching conversations after a course one of the most useful follow-ups you can add. There is more on [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4) and on [treating transfer as a design problem](t:5.1).

**Managers can coach too.** Teaching managers to ask good questions and follow up on practice puts coaching into the working week at no extra cost. Done badly, it becomes another meeting. There is more on [teaching managers to coach](t:2.46) and on [coaching with questions, not answers](t:5.5).

items: **Set goals at the start, and check them at the end.** Goal attainment is where coaching shows its largest effect, and it gives you something to measure.
**Ask for more than self-report.** A manager's view before and after, or one business measure, makes the case far stronger.
**Know where coaching stops.** Coaching is not therapy. Agree how a coach refers someone on. There is more on [knowing your professional limits](t:4.16).
**Check the coach, not the credential alone.** Ask for references from clients like yours.

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **Coaching is the natural second half of a retreat.** The retreat builds the skill, the group and the plan. Two or three coaching conversations over the following two months help each person use it at work. Selling them together answers the obvious objection to retreats, that it all fades once people are back at their desks. Group coaching with the retreat cohort keeps the cost down and the connections alive.

ideas.title: What finance will accept: making the business case for training
ideas.standfirst: Training has a credibility problem with the people who sign the budget. Most organisations do not measure business results, and those that try often claim more than they can show. This piece sets out what the research says training can achieve, and what kind of case a finance director will believe.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Well-designed training works, on average.** A pooling of 1,152 effect sizes found medium to large effects on learning, on behaviour at work and on results.
**Most buyers do not believe it.** Only a quarter of respondents to a McKinsey survey said their training measurably improved business performance.
**Few organisations check.** In ATD's research, about a third evaluated business results to any extent, and about one in six measured return on investment.
**Finance trusts a small, careful claim over a big one.** A baseline, a comparison and the business's own numbers beat any return-on-investment percentage.

sections.h: The case for training is better than its reputation
p: **Training in organisations has a real effect.** Arthur and colleagues pooled 1,152 effect sizes from studies of organisational training. The average effects were medium to large and similar whether the measure was learning, behaviour at work or results, at about 0.6 of a standard deviation. The method and the skill being trained mattered. The evidence that training can work is not the problem. There is more on [what training can do, on average](t:2.28).

**The reputation comes from what most training is like.** McKinsey found only one-quarter of respondents said their training programmes measurably improved business performance, and that most companies did not track returns. Its explanation was not poor content but poor conditions: people who did not see why they needed the skill, leaders who were not involved, and nothing to reinforce it back at work.

**Satisfaction scores prove almost nothing.** A pooling of studies found how much people liked a course had little relationship with what they learned or did afterwards. Finance teams know this, which is why a smile-sheet average does not move them. There is more on [using Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof](t:6.2).

**Big return-on-investment numbers invite disbelief.** A claim that a two-day course returned 400% will be taken apart in the first question: how do you know it was the course? Isolating the effect of training from everything else was one of the top barriers L&D professionals named in ATD's research. There is more on [separating the effect of training from everything else](t:6.6).

**A number the business already tracks.** Conversion rate, time to competence, error rate, staff turnover in the first year. If the measure lives in the client's own systems, nobody has to trust your survey. McKinsey's own example was a retailer whose pilot stores improved conversion by 150 basis points after training was redesigned around real store data. There is more on [showing the value in the client's own terms](t:6.8).

**A baseline and a comparison.** Measure before, and compare trained people with similar people not yet trained. A pilot that rolls out in waves gives you a comparison group for free. There is more on [running a pilot before you roll out](t:2.52).

**A conservative estimate, shown with its working.** State the cost, the change you saw, the share you are willing to attribute to training, and the assumptions. Finance will argue with your assumptions. That is fine, because it means they are reading the case rather than dismissing it. There is more on [building the cost and benefit case](t:6.15).

**Stories that are checked.** The Success Case Method finds the people who used the training most and least, and asks what made the difference. A verified story about one team's results is often more persuasive than an average. There is more on [using the Success Case Method](t:6.13).

**Match the effort to the stakes.** A small course needs a light check. A large programme needs a proper comparison. There is more on [matching the evaluation to the stakes](t:6.11).
**Training is rarely the only cause.** Say so first. It makes the rest of the case more believable.

p: **Retreats are expensive per head, so they get the hardest questions.** Agree with the sponsor, before you design, the one or two business measures the retreat is meant to move, and when you will look at them again. Offer to run the first cohort as a pilot with a comparison group. A modest result that holds up is worth more for the next sale than a dazzling one nobody believes.

ideas.title: What the best learning teams measure
ideas.standfirst: Almost every learning team measures whether people liked the course. Few measure whether people work differently afterwards. This piece sets out what organisations actually measure, why the easy measures mislead, and what the teams that do this well track instead.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Most teams stop at reaction and quiz scores.** In ATD's research, about eight in ten measured reaction and learning, about half measured behaviour at work, and fewer than four in ten measured results.
**Reaction tells you little.** How much people liked a course had little relationship with what they learned or did.
**The best teams decide the behaviour first.** They agree what people should do differently, then go and look for it.
**They measure less, better.** A light check on most programmes and a proper evaluation on the few that matter.

p: **The further from the room, the less it is measured.** ATD's 2019 research found 83% of organisations measured learners' reactions and 80% measured learning. 54% measured whether people used the skills at work, 38% measured business results and 16% measured return on investment. An earlier ATD study found only about a third evaluated business results to any extent.

**The reasons are practical.** L&D professionals named the difficulty of separating the effect of training from everything else, and a lack of time, data and skills. These are real obstacles. They are also why measures of reaction fill the gap: they are easy, and they always look good.

**Liking a course and learning from it are different things.** A pooling of studies by Alliger and colleagues found reactions had little relationship with learning or with behaviour at work. Courses that feel smooth can teach less than ones that feel effortful, because effort is often a sign of learning. There is more on [not trusting how fluent the room looks](t:1.4).

**Attendance and completion count activity, not change.** A completed e-learning module tells you someone reached the end. It says nothing about what they can now do. There is more on [not mistaking activity for learning](t:6.7).

**They agree the behaviour before they design.** What should people do differently, where, and how would anyone notice? Writing it down before design keeps everyone honest. There is more on [deciding what you will measure before you design](t:6.1).

**They look for behaviour at work.** Short observation, a manager's check, a work sample or a system record a month or two later. One good measure beats five survey items. There is more on [measuring what people do differently](t:6.4) and on [going back later to see what stuck](t:6.5).

**They use a richer scale than the four levels.** Kirkpatrick's levels are useful words. Thalheimer's Learning-Transfer Evaluation Model splits them further and makes the point that attendance and reaction are not evidence of learning at all. There is more on [using Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof](t:6.2).
**They report results people will read.** One page, the result first, in the business's own terms. There is more on [reporting results people will read](t:6.10).

items: **Keep the reaction survey short and useful.** Ask about relevance and confidence to use, not about the lunch. There is more on [asking better questions on the feedback form](t:6.3).
**Match the effort to the stakes.** Most programmes need a light check. A few deserve a proper study. There is more on [matching the evaluation to the stakes](t:6.11).
**Measurement needs access.** Agree with the client, up front, what data you will need and who will provide it. There is more on [getting the data you need from the client](t:6.12).

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **A retreat's feedback scores will always be high.** Good food, beautiful surroundings and a group that has bonded produce glowing reactions. That is exactly why they prove little. Build one behaviour measure into every retreat, such as a manager check-in six weeks later on the plan each person made, and report it. It will set you apart from competitors who only send the satisfaction scores.

ideas.title: What training can borrow from hospitality, theatre and games
ideas.standfirst: Hotels design for how a stay will be remembered. Theatres rehearse until the hard moments run themselves. Game designers keep people trying when they fail. Training borrows from all three, sometimes well and sometimes badly. This piece sorts the borrowing that has evidence behind it from the borrowing that does not.

short.heading: The short version
items: **People remember the best moment and the end.** A pooling of 174 effect sizes found the peak and the end of an experience shape how people later judge it, and length barely matters.

**Game elements help a little, and the right ones help more.** Gamified learning had small positive effects, largest on what people learned. Story and working with others made the difference to behaviour.
**Theatre's tools are promising but thinly tested.** Improvisation training has small studies behind it, mostly on creativity and confidence.
**Hospitality's best idea is a map, not a script.** Mapping every step a guest takes, and fixing the friction, is craft rather than science, and it works.

sections.h: Hospitality: design for how it will be remembered
p: **People judge an experience by its peak and its end.** Kahneman and colleagues first showed it with medical procedures and cold water. A 2022 meta-analysis of 174 effect sizes found the effect large and robust: when people look back on an experience, the most intense moment and the final moment count for more than the rest, and how long it lasted counts for very little. The research is about how experiences are remembered and rated, not about how much is learned. For a course, that means the final hour and one standout moment will shape what people say about it, and whether they recommend it. There is more on [planning a peak and a proper ending](t:2.18).

**Good hotels map the whole stay.** The craft of service design is to list every step a guest takes, from booking to the drive home, and fix the ones that frustrate. For training that starts with the joining email and ends with the follow-up. Nobody has tested journey mapping as a cause of better learning. It is still the quickest way to find out why people arrive late and annoyed. There is more on [mapping every step from first email to follow-up](t:2.17).

sections.h: Theatre: rehearse, and say yes, and
p: **Rehearsal is theatre's oldest lesson for trainers.** Actors run the hard scenes until they hold under pressure, and run the technical rehearsal so that nothing surprises them on the night. Aviation and medicine reached the same idea through simulation, and that is where the evidence is. There is more in [What good looks like today](insight:what-good-looks-like-today) and on [rehearsing what could go wrong](t:4.13).

**Improvisation is popular in workplace training and thinly studied.** A controlled field study by West, Hoff and Carlsson tested playful improvisation with 93 people from nine organisations, measuring creativity, playfulness and psychological safety. Other studies are small, often without comparison groups, and mostly about confidence and creativity rather than job performance. Use it to loosen a group and practise listening. Do not sell it as proven. There is more on [using play on purpose](t:1.25).

**Game elements help a little.** Sailer and Homner pooled experimental studies of gamified learning. They found small positive effects on what people learned, on motivation and on behaviour. The effect on learning held up in the more rigorous studies. The effects on motivation and behaviour were less stable.

**Story and company matter more than points.** For behaviour, gamification worked better when it included a story or setting and when people worked with others, and competition worked best when it was combined with collaboration. Points, badges and leaderboards added on their own are the weakest version. There is more on [using game elements only where they help](t:2.22).

items: **Borrow the method, not the costume.** A course with a hotel's welcome and no practice is a nice day, not training.
**Memorable is not the same as learned.** The peak-end rule tells you how people will rate a course. Use it, and keep the practice that does the teaching.
**Test borrowed ideas on a small group first.** What delights one audience embarrasses another.

business.heading: What this means for a retreat business
p: **A retreat is a hospitality product as well as a learning one.** Buyers will judge it partly the way they judge a hotel: the welcome, the food, the best evening and the last morning. Design those on purpose. Then make sure the peak is something people did together, not only a good dinner, and that the end sends them back to work with a plan. There is more on [planning the return to work](t:8.17).

ideas.title: What learners expect now: the consumer trends reshaping training
ideas.standfirst: People learn from YouTube before breakfast, use AI tools their employer never gave them, and choose jobs partly on how much they will grow. This digest gathers the research on what learners now expect from training, and what that means for the courses and retreats you design.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Learning has gone consumer.** People already teach themselves from video and search, on their own time. Training now competes with free, instant, good-enough help.
**AI arrived before the training did.** Three in four knowledge workers said they used AI at work in 2024, and most brought their own tools. People expect help that is personal and immediate.

**Growth matters more than ladders.** Younger workers rank learning among the top reasons they choose an employer, but few aim for senior leadership. They want skills, progress and practice on real work.
**People still want people.** The same surveys rate mentoring, peer learning and learning on the job above formal courses. That is the opening for live, human, well-designed experiences.

p: **People teach themselves, constantly.** In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey, about half of US adults who use YouTube said it was very important for figuring out how to do things they had not done before. A survey commissioned by Google across ten European countries found 64% felt YouTube helped them learn skills for personal or professional advancement. That second figure comes from YouTube's owner, so treat it as a signal rather than a measurement.

**The bar is set outside work.** Consumer research by McKinsey in 2021 found that 71% of consumers expected companies to personalise their interactions, and 76% were frustrated when that did not happen. That was about shopping, not learning. But the people on your course are the same people, and a generic, one-size course feels dated to them in the way a generic advert does.

**Personal does not mean learning styles.** The useful kind of personalisation is by role, prior knowledge and goal. Sorting people by preferred style does not hold up. There is more on [the big myths](t:1.10) and on [finding out who is in the room](t:1.29).

sections.h: AI arrived before the training did
p: **Most knowledge workers already use it.** Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries found 75% of knowledge workers said they used generative AI at work, and 78% of those users brought their own tools rather than waiting for their employer. In Deloitte's 2025 survey of younger workers, about three-quarters expected generative AI to change how they work within a year.

**Expectations shift with it.** People who can ask an AI tool to explain something at eleven at night will expect training to give quick answers and save live time for what a tool cannot do: practice, judgement and feedback from people. There is more on [designing an AI literacy and adoption programme](t:7.13).

**Learning helps people choose an employer.** Deloitte's 2025 survey of 23,482 Gen Z and millennial workers in 44 countries found learning and development among the top three reasons they chose their current employer. Only 6% said their main career goal was a leadership position.

**Career progress drives learning.** LinkedIn's 2025 Workplace Learning Report names progress towards career goals as people's top motivation to learn. Learning that shows where it leads competes better for attention than learning that does not.

**Practice and mentors rank highest.** In Deloitte's survey, 88% of Gen Zs and 89% of millennials said on-the-job learning and practical experience mattered for their development, and more than 80% rated mentoring, peer learning and feedback as helpful. Formal training programmes were on the list too, but not at the top.

**Experiences are a growing market.** Pine and Gilmore argued in 1998 that experiences are a distinct economic offering, beyond goods and services. The Global Wellness Institute put wellness tourism at about US$982 billion in 2025, up 11.4% in a year. One detail matters for a training business: in its 2025 report, workplace wellness was the only wellness market that shrank, by 1.5% from 2023 to 2024. Buyers are paying for experiences that do something, not for wellbeing perks.

**This is the opening for well-designed live learning.** Free content covers information. What people value and cannot get from a video is practice with feedback, people to learn with, and time that is protected for it. There is more on [the case for taking people away](insight:why-take-people-away).

ideas.title: Attention is the scarce resource: what learners expect now, and how to hold it
ideas.standfirst: Is there e-learning fatigue? Are attention spans really shrinking? What do people want from training when their working day is broken into two-minute pieces? This digest gathers the research, separates what is measured from what is repeated, and ends with what holds attention in a session today.

short.heading: The short version
items: **Attention spans have not been shown to collapse.** The eight-second goldfish figure has no source. What has been measured is that people switch between screens far more often than they used to: on average every 47 seconds in recent studies, against about two and a half minutes in 2004.

**The working day is the problem.** Heavy users of Microsoft 365 are interrupted about every two minutes in core hours, and fewer than four in ten learning professionals say employees get time away from their job to learn. Learners arrive fragmented and short of time.

**"E-learning fatigue" is real in parts.** Video-call fatigue is measured and well described. Low completion of long, open online courses is measured. Fatigue with digital learning as such is mostly anecdote, and well-designed online learning teaches as well as a classroom.

**Attention is held by design, not by length.** Active tasks, short recall checks between segments, short videos, protected time and a clear link to the learner's own progress all have research behind them. A stopwatch rule does not.

p: **The goldfish figure has no source.** The claim that people now have an eight-second attention span, shorter than a goldfish, spread from a 2015 marketing report by Microsoft Canada. The report took the figure from a website called Statistic Brain, and journalists who traced it found no research behind it. In a 2022 King's College London survey, half of UK adults still believed it. There is more on [testing a claim before you repeat it](t:1.11).

**What has been measured is switching.** Gloria Mark and colleagues have logged how long office workers stay on one screen before moving to another. In 2004 it was about two and a half minutes. By about 2012 it was 75 seconds, and in studies from 2016 onwards it averaged 47 seconds. That measures how often people switch at work, with email and messages always open. It does not measure whether people can concentrate when the setting allows it.

**People feel more distracted.** In the King's College survey, 49% said their attention span felt shorter than it used to be and 23% disagreed. The researchers point out that without long-term studies nobody can say whether attention spans have actually declined. Feeling distracted is still real, and it is what learners bring into the room.

**There is no fixed span to design to.** A review of lecture studies found no good evidence for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes, and attention varied more with the teacher than with the format. There is more on [attention and mind wandering](t:1.33).

sections.h: The working day learners come from
p: **Interruptions are constant for many office workers.** Microsoft's 2025 analysis of anonymised Microsoft 365 data found the most heavily contacted fifth of users were interrupted by a meeting, email or message about every two minutes during core hours, around 275 times across a full day. Reports often quote it as the average worker. Microsoft's own note says it describes that heavily contacted group.

**Time to learn is scarce.** In the CIPD's 2023 survey of 1,108 learning professionals, 51% said people managers encourage participation in learning, but only 39% said employees are given time away from their day-to-day role to take part. LinkedIn's 2025 Workplace Learning Report found managers and employees too stretched to focus on development, and only 15% of employees said their manager had helped them build a career plan in the previous six months.

**Career progress is why people choose to learn.** The same LinkedIn report names progress towards career goals as people's number one motivation to learn. Learning that shows how it moves someone forward competes better for scarce attention than learning that does not. There is more on [why people value a task](t:1.34).

**Video-call fatigue is measured.** Researchers at Stanford built a scale for it and surveyed 10,591 people. More daily video calling went with more fatigue. Women reported more than men, with about one in seven women feeling very or extremely fatigued after calls against about one in twenty men, partly because they had longer meetings with shorter breaks and partly because of seeing themselves on screen all day. There is more on [designing against video-call fatigue](t:4.8).

**Long, open online courses lose most people.** Data from Harvard and MIT's open online courses showed completion rates stayed low and did not improve over six years, and most learners did not come back after their first year. These were free, optional courses, so low completion partly reflects people sampling and leaving. Workplace e-learning that is required gets completed, which says nothing about whether it was learned.

**Video holds attention for a few minutes.** A study of 6.9 million video sessions on edX found engagement dropped sharply after about six minutes, and that videos with a personal feel held people better than polished studio lectures.

**Digital learning as such is not the problem.** When online and classroom courses use the same methods, they teach facts equally well. What tires people is long, passive, screen-based time added to an already crowded day. The answer is better design and protected time, not a retreat from digital. There is more on [comparing online and classroom](t:3.11) and on [completion figures](t:6.7).

**Make people do something.** A pooling of 225 studies in university science courses found that students in traditional lectures were 1.5 times more likely to fail than students in courses with active learning, and exam scores were about 6% higher with active learning.

**Put a short recall check between segments.** In an online lecture experiment, people who answered a short quiz after each segment reported mind wandering at 19% of checks, against 41% for people who were not tested, and they learned more.

**Keep videos short and personal.** Cut recorded input into pieces of a few minutes, and use the live time for interaction. There is more on [blending on purpose](t:3.6) and on [keeping live time for interaction](t:4.10).

**Protect the time, not just the content.** Learning booked into the gaps of a fragmented day loses to the next message. Ask the manager to protect it, close email for the session, and say plainly why.
**Show the link to the learner's own progress.** In the first five minutes, say what people will be able to do and why it matters for their work and career.
**Plan the energy of the day.** Put demanding work where energy is highest and change the activity when it drops. There is more on [putting the hard content where the energy is](t:2.14).

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **Check what a figure measures.** Screen switching is not concentration, a survey of learning professionals is not a survey of learners, and the heaviest fifth of email users is not the average worker.

**Vendor reports have something to sell.** LinkedIn, Microsoft and platform providers publish useful data, and every report also makes a case for their product. Use the figures, and say who produced them.
**Completion is not learning.** High completion of required e-learning and low completion of free courses both say more about the setting than about what people learned.
**Most of the attention research uses students.** Workplace evidence is thinner. Treat the methods as good bets and check them with your own groups.
**Fatigue is a design signal, not a learner failing.** When people drift, change the format, the length or the time of day before you blame the audience.

business.heading: What this means for the training you design
p: **Design for people who arrive fragmented.** Open by settling the room: phones away for a reason, one clear goal, and a first task within ten minutes. There is more on [designing for people who arrive distracted](t:4.21).
**Spend live time on doing.** Put information into short recordings and reading, and use the time together for practice, discussion and feedback.

**Sell protected time as part of the offer.** Ask clients to block the time, brief managers and keep the session free of email. A training retreat takes this to its limit, which is part of [the case for taking people away](insight:why-take-people-away).
**Keep a running file of the research.** The figures here will date. Recheck the annual reports each year and add new studies as they appear.

ideas.title: The neuroscience of the retreat: what the brain science supports, and what it does not
ideas.standfirst: Retreat brochures are full of brains: cortisol falling, dopamine rising, the default mode network switching on, oxytocin bonding the team. This piece checks each claim against the research, so you can talk about the brain honestly, and know when to stop.

short.heading: The short version
items: **The behaviour is better evidenced than the brain.** Sleep, stress, reflection, novelty and moving together have useful research behind them. The brain pictures in brochures usually go well beyond it.
**Some brain stories are real but small.** Time in nature, exercise and stress all affect thinking, with modest, short-lived effects in laboratory studies of students.
**Some are hype.** "Oxytocin builds trust" did not survive scrutiny. "Dopamine hits" and "amygdala hijack" are metaphors, not findings.
**Say what happens, not what the brain does.** "Time to sleep between sessions" is honest and true. "Rewires your brain" is neither.

p: **A brain picture makes any claim look scientific.** Brain language sounds precise and is hard for a buyer to check, which is why it spreads through training and wellness marketing. There is more on [why smart people believe brain myths](t:1.9). The test is simple: does the claim tell you to do something different from what the behavioural research already says? If not, the brain story adds risk and nothing else.

**Stress affects memory, in both directions.** A pooling of 113 studies with 6,216 people found that stress shortly before or during learning usually impaired memory, unless it came very close to the learning and was related to it. Stress just after learning often improved memory. Stress just before recall impaired it. Long-running stress is a different matter and harms learning. There is more on [taking needless stress out of the room](t:1.13).

**Brochure cortisol figures are usually wrong.** This site traced one infographic claiming nature cuts cortisol "by up to 38%". The values on its chart were about a hundred times too high to be saliva measurements. Small studies do find lower stress hormone levels after time in nature, but no study supports a headline percentage for a retreat.

sections.h: Rest and the default mode network
p: **There is a brain network for turning inward.** A review by Immordino-Yang and colleagues describes the default mode network, which is active when people rest and let their minds wander. It links that network to recalling memories, imagining the future and reflecting on meaning. The review draws mostly on correlational research and argues for more study, not for a particular method.

**The useful lesson is behavioural.** Time to reflect helps learning, and experiments on reflection support it without any brain imaging. A retreat that builds in quiet time and prompts for reflection is doing the right thing. Saying it "activates the default mode network" adds nothing a buyer can use. There is more on [giving people time alone to reflect](t:8.28).

**New places may help memory.** An influential model by Lisman and Grace describes a loop in which novelty detected by the hippocampus triggers dopamine that helps new information get stored. Animal studies show that exploring a new environment strengthens memory processes. A small number of human studies, some in virtual reality, find that exploring something new improves recall.

**The leap to retreats is a long one.** The human studies are small laboratory experiments. They support the idea that a new setting is no barrier to learning and may help a little. They do not support "dopamine hits" as a selling point. There is more on [making people curious before you tell them](t:1.26).

**Oxytocin is not a trust switch.** A critical review by Nave, Camerer and McCullough found that the best-known finding, that sniffing oxytocin increases trust, has not replicated well. They concluded the evidence does not reliably link oxytocin to human trust. Drop it from any pitch.

**Moving together has better support.** Pooled experiments on moving in time with others, such as walking, rowing or dancing together, found medium effects on helpful behaviour and small to medium effects on feeling bonded. Some researchers warn that expectations may explain part of it. It is a behavioural finding and needs no brain story.

**Awe may turn attention outward.** Piff and colleagues ran five studies in which feeling awe, including in front of tall trees, went with more generous and helpful behaviour. The authors link it to a feeling of a smaller self. It is a reasonable reason to take people somewhere beautiful, stated modestly.

**Sleep is the strongest brain story.** Memories are strengthened and reorganised during sleep, and a lost night before or after learning weakens memory. A retreat that protects sleep has the brain on its side. There is more on [protecting sleep](t:1.12).

**Exercise and nature help a little.** One bout of exercise has a small, real effect on thinking. Time in nature brings small, short-lived gains in some measures of attention. Both are worth building in. Neither is a reason to promise better learning. There is more on [using nature and daylight](t:1.16).

items.note: Stress before or during learning usually impaired memory; stress just after learning often helped; stress before recall impaired it (Shields and colleagues, 2017).
items.mind: Remove needless stress, especially before practice and recall. Short challenge is not the enemy.

items.note: The figure traced on this site had chart values about a hundred times too high for saliva. Small studies do find lower stress hormone levels after time in nature.

items.name: Default mode network
items.offers: "Retreats switch on the brain's reflective network."
items.note: The network active at rest is linked to memory, imagining the future and reflection, in mostly correlational research (Immordino-Yang and colleagues, 2012).
items.mind: Build in reflection. Leave the network out of the brochure.
links: Give people time alone to reflect

items.name: Novelty and dopamine
items.offers: "New places release dopamine that boosts learning."
items.note: A strong model (Lisman and Grace, 2005) and animal studies, with a few small human experiments finding better recall after exploring something new.
items.mind: A new setting may help a little. "Dopamine hits" is marketing.
links: Make people curious before you tell them

items.name: Oxytocin and trust
items.offers: "Bonding releases oxytocin, the trust hormone."
items.note: The evidence does not reliably link oxytocin to human trust (Nave, Camerer and McCullough, 2015).
items.mind: Remove it. Build trust with the methods that work: safety, time and shared work.
links: Build trust before you ask for openness

items.name: Moving together
items.offers: "Moving in time together bonds a group."
items.note: Pooled experiments found a medium effect of moving in time together on helpful attitudes and behaviour (Rennung and Göritz, 2016). Expectations may explain part of it.
items.mind: Group walks and movement may help people bond. Keep them optional.
links: Offer movement sessions people can choose

items.name: Awe
items.offers: "Awe makes people more generous."
items.note: Feeling awe, including in front of tall trees, went with more generous and helpful behaviour (Piff and colleagues, 2015).
items.mind: A modest reason to choose a beautiful setting. Not a promise of a changed team.
links: Use the outdoors on a retreat, on purpose

items.name: Nature and attention
items.offers: "Nature restores the brain."
items.note: Reviews find small, short-lived gains in working memory and switching between tasks after time in nature (Stevenson and colleagues, 2018).
items.mind: Use nature for recovery between sessions. Do not promise better learning.
links: Use nature and daylight, and claim only what the evidence shows

items.name: Exercise and the brain
items.offers: "Exercise grows new brain cells."
items.note: One bout of exercise has a real but generally small effect on thinking (Chang and colleagues, 2012). Longer-term brain claims are promising and easy to overstate.
items.mind: Offer movement for energy. Leave brain growth out of it.
links: Use movement where it helps the learning

items.name: Amygdala hijack
items.offers: "Fear hijacks the thinking brain."
items.note: A popular phrase from Daniel Goleman's 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, not a research finding. Stress and threat do affect thinking, as the stress research shows.
items.mind: Talk about psychological safety, which has research behind it.
links: Make it safe to be wrong out loud

items.name: Rewiring the brain
items.offers: "Rewire your brain in a weekend."
items.note: All learning changes the brain in some sense. No research shows a retreat produces a special or lasting rewiring.
items.mind: Promise practice, plans and follow-up instead.
links: Promise the conditions, never the transformation

mind.heading: Things to bear in mind
items: **A brain claim is a health claim.** Advertising rules expect evidence for objective claims before you publish them. There is more on [describing the retreat honestly](t:9.7).
**Most studies used students in laboratories.** Workplace and retreat evidence is much thinner.
**Brain pictures persuade more than they should.** Leave them out of proposals unless they change what you will do.
**Clients will quote brain claims to you.** Agree with what is true, correct what is not, and say what you will do instead.

business.heading: What this means for your retreats
p: **Lead with what happens.** Sleep, quiet time, practice, shared meals, walks and evenings are all easy to describe and backed by research about behaviour.
**Use one brain fact, well.** Sleep helping memory is the strongest. Use it to explain the early finishes, and stop there.
**Be the honest one.** In a market full of dopamine and cortisol, a provider who can explain what the science does and does not say will stand out to serious buyers.
